h1: Investor Renovation Contractor in Fayetteville, AR
intro: Fayetteville is not a distressed-house market, and that changes how renovation math works. Northwest Arkansas has grown steadily for years on the University of Arkansas, Walmart, Tyson, J.B. Hunt and the businesses around them, and older houses near campus and downtown rarely sell cheap. Margins come from buying the right house, renovating it efficiently and competing well against new construction, student housing complexes and a deep pool of local contractors. Genstone Construction renovates in Fayetteville and across Washington and Benton counties for flippers, BRRRR and rental investors, owners of student duplexes and fourplexes, FHA 203(k) buyers and REO asset managers. We coordinate vetted, licensed local trades, and a designated field manager runs each project from walk-through to final billing. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review prices repairs against your ARV, rent or refinance target before you commit, and every job comes with a line-item scope, a draw schedule, City of Fayetteville permits handled, remote documentation and no upfront payment.
housingStock:
Fayetteville's older housing sits on hills. The town grew up around the university and the downtown square on the edge of the Ozark Plateau, so even in-town neighborhoods have slopes, rock outcrops and lots that drop off behind the house. Washington-Willow, just north of downtown, holds the city's best-known collection of late nineteenth- and early twentieth-century homes, from Victorian and Colonial Revival houses to Craftsman bungalows. Mount Nord and Mount Sequoyah climb the ridges east of downtown with houses from the early and middle twentieth century, many with walkout lower levels or partial basements cut into the slope.

Wilson Park and the streets around it carry modest cottages and bungalows from the 1920s through the 1950s, popular with university faculty and young professionals. Haskell Heights and the neighborhoods north and west of campus mix mid-century ranches with a large stock of duplexes, triplexes and small apartment buildings built from the 1960s through the 1990s for students. South Fayetteville and the Walker Park area have older, smaller houses on varied lots, while Hyland Park and the east and west edges of town are dominated by subdivisions from the 1970s onward.

Two things shape almost every rehab here. The first is ground conditions. Rocky, cherty soils and shallow limestone in parts of the region make excavation, sewer repairs and foundation work harder, and steep lots push stormwater toward houses and into crawlspaces and basements. Parts of Northwest Arkansas also have karst features. The second is age and use. Older houses carry the usual pre-1978 issues of lead paint, outdated wiring and galvanized plumbing, and student rentals near campus have often absorbed decades of hard use with minimal reinvestment. Many of those buildings need full interior renovations and system replacements rather than cosmetic refreshes.

commonIssues.title: Hillside water and wet lower levels
commonIssues.body: Sloped lots across Fayetteville send runoff toward foundations, and walkout basements and crawlspaces on the downhill side are where it ends up. Investors find damp or flooded lower levels, efflorescence on block walls, rotted sills, mold and failing retaining walls. A durable fix usually starts outside with gutters, downspouts, grading and sometimes a curtain or French drain, then moves to interior drainage and waterproofing. Finishing a lower level before the water is managed is money spent twice.

commonIssues.title: Rock, slopes and difficult excavation
commonIssues.body: Shallow rock and chert make digging slow and expensive in parts of the city. Replacing a sewer lateral, adding a footing, setting a retaining wall or regrading a yard can cost more than an investor used to flat clay-soil markets might expect. We have local trades look at site conditions during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review so excavation-heavy items are priced realistically rather than guessed at from another region's numbers.

commonIssues.title: Worn-out student rentals
commonIssues.body: Duplexes and small apartment buildings near campus often show heavy wear: damaged doors and trim, stained or broken flooring, worn kitchens and baths, failing HVAC units and electrical that has been overloaded with modern electronics. Many have had only quick turns for years. Bringing them up to a competitive standard usually means full interior renovation unit by unit, with durable materials chosen to survive the next round of tenants.

commonIssues.title: Freeze and ice damage
commonIssues.body: Northwest Arkansas winters are colder than the rest of the state, with ice storms and hard freezes that can split pipes in exterior walls, crawlspaces and vacant houses. The region's 2009 ice storm and more recent cold snaps damaged roofs, trees and plumbing. We check for past freeze damage, insulate exposed supply lines and recommend winterization on any property that will sit vacant during colder months.

commonIssues.title: Older systems and unpermitted conversions
commonIssues.body: Pre-war houses near downtown may still have knob-and-tube wiring, galvanized supply lines and undersized panels. Mid-century houses near campus were sometimes chopped into extra bedrooms or units without permits. Those changes cause problems with zoning, egress, fire safety and insurance. We look for signs of unpermitted work, confirm what the city recognizes and plan the scope so the finished property has a clean record.

investorMarket:
Fayetteville's investor market is shaped by the university and by regional growth. Near campus, in Haskell Heights and the neighborhoods north and west of the university, small multifamily buildings and single-family houses rented to students are the main investor product. Demand is steady, but the competition includes newer purpose-built student housing complexes with amenities, so older buildings need solid renovations to hold rents. Leases often follow the academic calendar, with move-ins concentrated in late summer.

Downtown, Wilson Park, Washington-Willow, Mount Nord and Mount Sequoyah attract owner-occupant buyers who want walkability, character and proximity to Dickson Street and the square. These neighborhoods can support quality flips, but buyers are discerning and expect structural, drainage and systems work to be done well. Historic character is part of the value.

On the edges of town and in neighboring Springdale, Farmington and Johnson, older ranches and 1970s through 1990s houses appeal to families and workforce households who are priced out of new construction. Those houses suit BRRRR, long-term rentals and FHA 203(k) purchases, especially for buyers who want an established neighborhood rather than a new subdivision.

The main challenges are acquisition price, competition from new construction and local zoning rules. Short-term rentals are regulated, and occupancy limits on unrelated tenants can affect student rental plans. Our Pre-Offer Rehab Review puts repair costs next to realistic resale values or rents so you can decide whether the strategy fits the specific house.
permits:
Inside city limits, building, electrical, plumbing and mechanical permits are handled by the City of Fayetteville's Development Services department through its building safety division, under the city's Unified Development Code. Permits are typically required for structural repairs, foundation work, roofing, electrical and plumbing changes, HVAC replacement, additions, decks, retaining walls above certain heights, conversions and window or door changes that alter openings. Grading and stormwater rules can also come into play on sloped lots when a project changes drainage or adds impervious surface.

Zoning matters a great deal for investors here. Adding or recognizing units, converting a house to multiple units, or changing how a property is rented can involve zoning review, and the city regulates short-term rentals through its own licensing process. Rules on the number of unrelated occupants can limit how a house near campus is leased, so check them before planning bedroom counts. Designated historic properties may involve review by the city's historic district commission.

Springdale, Rogers, Bentonville, Farmington and other nearby cities run separate permit offices. Residential remodeling and home improvement jobs in Arkansas above certain contract amounts must be performed by contractors licensed with the state's Contractors Licensing Board. For Fayetteville projects, Genstone brings in trades with the right Arkansas licenses, handles the permit filings, books inspections and requires lien waivers before releasing each draw.
climate:
Fayetteville sits higher and farther north than most of Arkansas, so it gets real winters along with hot, humid summers. Snow and ice storms occur most years, and hard freezes can damage exposed plumbing, stress roofs and bring down trees onto houses. Exterior work like roofing, painting and concrete is easier to schedule in spring and fall, and concrete and masonry need protection from freezing temperatures in winter.

Spring brings severe thunderstorms, hail, high winds and occasional tornadoes. Heavy rain on hilly terrain produces fast runoff and flash flooding along creeks, so drainage around the house and in the crawlspace or basement deserves attention in every scope. Freeze-thaw cycles crack concrete steps, walks and driveways and can loosen mortar in older masonry. Summer heat and humidity require climate control for drywall, paint and flooring installation, especially in older houses without central air.

faqs.q: Does it make sense to renovate older houses in Fayetteville when there is so much new construction?
faqs.a: It can, but the renovation has to compete. Buyers and renters compare older houses with new builds that offer modern layouts, efficient systems and warranties. Older homes win on location, lot character and proximity to campus, downtown and Dickson Street, so the renovation should protect those strengths while fixing drainage, systems and layout problems. Our Pre-Offer Rehab Review compares repair costs with realistic values or rents to check whether a specific house can compete.

faqs.q: Do you work in Springdale, Rogers and Bentonville?
faqs.a: Yes. Genstone coordinates vetted, licensed local contractors across Northwest Arkansas, including Springdale, Rogers, Bentonville, Farmington, Johnson, Prairie Grove, Elkins and Lowell. Each city has its own permit office, zoning code and inspection schedule, and your field manager handles permits in the correct jurisdiction. Housing in Bentonville and Rogers skews newer than Fayetteville's older in-town neighborhoods, so scopes there tend to focus on systems, finishes and wear rather than structure.

faqs.q: Can you renovate a student rental near the University of Arkansas before the fall move-in?
faqs.a: Often, yes, but timing needs planning. Student leases tend to end and begin around late summer, which leaves a short window for unit renovations. We scope and order materials before tenants move out, line up trades in advance and phase work so the units with the most work start first. Larger projects, such as system replacements or exterior work, can be scheduled for other parts of the year when tenants are in place.

faqs.q: Can I manage a Fayetteville renovation remotely?
faqs.a: Yes. Many investors in Northwest Arkansas live elsewhere, including parents who bought for a student and later kept the house as a rental. Your designated field manager coordinates local trades, handles permits and inspections and provides photos and milestone updates. You pay nothing before work starts, each draw follows finished work and the last payment waits for your sign-off. You make the decisions without driving to Fayetteville for every stage of the project.

fix-flip.title: Fix and Flip Contractor in Fayetteville, AR | Genstone
fix-flip.metaDescription: Fayetteville, AR fix and flip renovations for Wilson Park, Mount Sequoyah and Washington-Willow: drainage, systems and finishes that compete with new builds.
fix-flip.h1: Fix and Flip Renovations in Fayetteville, AR
fix-flip.intro: A Fayetteville flip competes with new construction on one side and with the city's best-restored older homes on the other. Buyers looking near Wilson Park, Mount Sequoyah or Washington-Willow have usually toured a few new builds out west or in Farmington before they see your house, and they expect the older home to give them character and location without leaving them a list of problems. Genstone writes Fayetteville flip scopes to meet that standard. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review checks drainage, foundation, roof, wiring and plumbing alongside your comps and ARV. The scope we produce includes labor, materials and a draw schedule, often with more than one finish plan. A designated field manager coordinates licensed local trades, handles City of Fayetteville permits and keeps the project on pace so carrying costs stay in line.

sections.h2: Competing with new construction in Northwest Arkansas
sections.body:
In much of the country, a renovated older house competes mostly with other renovated older houses. In Fayetteville, it also competes with a steady supply of new homes and townhomes across the metro. Those houses offer open plans, efficient systems, attached garages and builder warranties, so a flip has to answer the question of why a buyer should choose an older home instead.

The answer is usually location and character: walking distance to the square, Dickson Street or campus, mature trees, hillside views and houses with architectural detail that new subdivisions do not have. A good flip leans into those strengths while removing the reasons buyers hesitate. That means modernizing the kitchen and baths, improving layout and storage where the structure allows, upgrading HVAC and electrical so the house feels as comfortable as new construction and dealing with water problems in basements and crawlspaces. We help you decide where the money creates the most value, and we can prepare more than one finish plan so you can compare cost against what renovated comps nearby have actually sold for.

sections.h2: Drainage, rock and structure on Fayetteville lots
sections.body:
The house inspectors in Fayetteville know what to look for on hillside properties: water marks on basement walls, damp crawlspaces, rotted sills, cracked block and leaning retaining walls. A flip that covers those issues with paint and new flooring tends to come apart at inspection. We start outside, finding where water enters and correcting it with gutters, downspout extensions, regrading and drains as needed. Then we evaluate the foundation and framing, repair any rot or movement and finish with interior waterproofing or a crawlspace vapor barrier.

Site conditions can change the price of that work. Shallow rock and chert can make trenching for a drain or replacing a sewer lateral much harder than in soft-soil markets, and retaining wall repairs on steep lots can be significant. We have local trades evaluate those items during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review so the budget reflects real conditions. Addressing them early protects your finishes, gives buyers documentation and reduces the risk of renegotiation after the buyer's inspection.

sections.h2: Finishes and schedule for Fayetteville buyers
sections.body:
Fayetteville buyers include university faculty and staff, healthcare workers, professionals employed across Northwest Arkansas and families relocating to the region. Many appreciate older homes but expect modern function. In Washington-Willow and Mount Nord, preserving original floors, trim, built-ins and porches typically supports value. In Wilson Park, buyers want cottages that feel light and updated without losing their charm. On Mount Sequoyah, a renovated walkout lower level with dry, usable space can add real appeal.

Scheduling matters because demand follows the seasons. Spring and summer bring more buyers, including families timing moves around the school year and university hires arriving before the fall semester. Winter weather can slow exterior work like roofing and concrete, so we plan those tasks early when a project starts in the fall. Your field manager orders long-lead items as soon as the scope is approved, coordinates permits and inspections and provides progress updates. Draws are tied to completed work, and the final payment follows your approval of the finished house.

faqs.q: Which Fayetteville neighborhoods work best for flips?
faqs.a: Wilson Park, Washington-Willow, Mount Nord, Mount Sequoyah and streets close to downtown and Dickson Street tend to attract owner-occupant buyers who value location and character. Some areas closer to campus may be better suited to rentals because of student demand and zoning limits. Our Pre-Offer Rehab Review compares repair costs with renovated sales near the specific house so you can see whether a flip makes sense there.

faqs.q: How do I make an older Fayetteville house compete with new construction?
faqs.a: Focus on what new houses cannot offer, such as location, mature trees and character, while fixing the things that make older homes feel like work. That usually means modern kitchens and baths, efficient HVAC, updated electrical, dry basements or crawlspaces and good storage. We can price more than one finish level so you can compare the cost of each upgrade with how much it moves your likely sale price.

faqs.q: Why do excavation and drainage costs run high in Fayetteville?
faqs.a: Many lots have slopes and shallow rock or chert, which makes trenching, regrading and sewer line work more labor-intensive than in soft-soil markets. Retaining walls on steep lots can also be expensive to rebuild. We have local trades look at site conditions during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review so these items are priced realistically before you commit to an offer. Knowing those numbers early keeps them out of your change orders.

brrrr.title: BRRRR Rehab Contractor in Fayetteville, AR | Genstone
brrrr.metaDescription: BRRRR renovation in Fayetteville, AR: ranches and duplexes rehabbed for the refinance appraisal and built for students, university staff and NWA workforce.
brrrr.intro: BRRRR in Fayetteville looks different than it does in low-cost markets. Purchase prices are higher, so the deals that work tend to be houses with obvious, fixable problems that keep retail buyers away: worn-out student rentals, mid-century ranches that were never updated, or older homes with water issues that scare off a conventional buyer. Renovated well, those houses can appraise strongly in a growing region and rent to students, university staff and workers employed across Northwest Arkansas. Genstone writes Fayetteville BRRRR scopes aimed at both the refinance and the long hold. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review compares repair costs with ARV and expected rents before you commit. A designated field manager runs licensed local crews and City of Fayetteville permits, and Genstone Financial can provide DSCR rental loans for the refinance if you want it handled within the same group of companies.

sections.h2: Finding the value gap in a growing market
sections.body:
In Fayetteville, the BRRRR opportunity rarely comes from a cheap purchase price. It comes from the gap between a house's condition and its location. A ranch near Wilson Park with a wet crawlspace, original electrical and a dated kitchen may sell below neighboring renovated houses because most buyers do not want the work. A duplex near campus that has been turned over quickly for years may be priced on its current rents rather than what it could earn after a real renovation.

Our Pre-Offer Rehab Review is built to measure that gap. We estimate repair costs, including drainage, structure and system work that site conditions can make more expensive, and compare them with renovated sales and achievable rents. The goal is to see whether the refinance will return enough of your capital to justify the deal. Appraisers here rely on recent nearby sales, and with active new construction in the region, it is important to compare your property with renovated older homes rather than with new builds in a different price tier.

sections.h2: Renovating for the appraisal and the tenant
sections.body:
Appraisers give the most weight to improvements they can see and verify: updated kitchens and baths, newer HVAC, a sound roof, quality flooring and a dry, structurally sound house. In Fayetteville, a basement or crawlspace that shows water problems can hurt both the appraisal and future tenant satisfaction, so drainage and moisture control are usually high on the BRRRR scope.

For tenants, durability is the priority. We favor waterproof plank flooring, washable paint in consistent colors, solid-core doors, durable counters and fixtures that are easy to repair. HVAC systems should be sized for both hot summers and real winters, and older houses without ductwork may benefit from ductless systems. Exterior work focuses on a sound roof, gutters that move water away from the house and siding and trim that resist moisture. We provide a completed-work summary with photos, permits and inspection results to help the appraiser understand the scope of the renovation and place the house among renovated comps.

Fayetteville renters fall into a few groups. Students near campus often sign leases on an academic cycle and share houses with roommates, which affects wear and bedroom layouts. University staff, healthcare workers and young professionals tend to want quieter houses near downtown, Wilson Park or the trail system. Workforce households employed across Northwest Arkansas look for affordable, well-maintained houses in established neighborhoods and nearby towns.

Your renovation should match the tenant you are targeting. Student rentals need extra durability and must respect the city's limits on unrelated occupants. Staff and professional rentals benefit from updated kitchens, good storage and outdoor space. Workforce rentals need reliable systems and low maintenance. Genstone Property Management can lease and manage the property after the renovation, and Genstone Financial offers DSCR rental loans, though both are optional. Our one-year workmanship warranty covers the renovation itself; tenant damage and normal wear are not included, which is why material choices matter from the beginning.

faqs.q: Can BRRRR work in Fayetteville with higher purchase prices?
faqs.a: It can, but the deal has to come from a value gap rather than a low price. Look for houses whose condition keeps most retail buyers away, such as water problems, dated systems or worn-out student rentals, in locations where renovated houses sell or rent well. Our Pre-Offer Rehab Review compares repair costs with ARV and rents so you can test whether the refinance returns enough capital before you buy.

faqs.q: What renovations matter most for a Fayetteville refinance appraisal?
faqs.a: Kitchens and baths, HVAC, roofing, flooring and a dry, structurally sound house carry the most weight. Water in a basement or crawlspace can drag down both the appraisal and future rents, so drainage and moisture work is usually a priority. A completed-work summary with permits and inspection results helps the appraiser understand the renovation and compare your house with similar updated homes nearby.

faqs.q: Can Genstone help with the BRRRR refinance and leasing?
faqs.a: Genstone Financial offers DSCR rental loans, fix-and-flip loans and lines of credit, and Genstone Property Management can lease and manage the property after the renovation. Both are optional. If you work with another lender or manager, we provide the scope, draw records and completion documentation they need. Your field manager focuses on finishing the Fayetteville renovation so the house is ready for appraisal and tenants.

rental-renovation.title: Rental Property Renovation in Fayetteville, AR | Genstone
rental-renovation.metaDescription: Single-family rental renovation in Fayetteville, AR: student and workforce rentals rebuilt for durability, dry lower levels and quick, documented turns.
rental-renovation.h1: Single-Family Rental Renovations in Fayetteville, AR
rental-renovation.intro: Fayetteville rental portfolios often combine houses near the University of Arkansas leased to students, older cottages and ranches near downtown rented to staff and young professionals, and houses in Springdale, Farmington or Johnson rented to workforce households. Each group has different wear patterns, but they share local conditions: hilly lots that push water toward foundations, cold winters, hot summers and a competitive rental market that includes newer complexes and townhomes. Genstone renovates and turns single-family rentals for individual landlords, funds and institutional owners across Northwest Arkansas. We create a portfolio standard suited to those conditions, coordinate vetted, licensed local contractors and handle permits and inspections. A designated field manager documents each property, and Genstone Field Services can provide inspections, occupied maintenance and turn and make-ready work between larger renovations.

sections.h2: A rental standard built for the Ozarks
sections.body:
A rental standard that works in a flat, warm market will miss problems here. Our Fayetteville standard starts with water and weather. Gutters and downspouts must carry water well away from the house, grading should slope away from the foundation and lower levels or crawlspaces need drainage, vapor barriers or dehumidification depending on conditions. Supply lines in exterior walls and crawlspaces are insulated, and hose bibs are frost-protected, because hard freezes are common.

Inside, we standardize on waterproof plank flooring, washable paint in consistent colors, durable cabinets and counters and fixtures with parts available locally. HVAC systems need to heat as well as cool; in older houses without ducts, ductless systems can be a practical upgrade. Electrical panels and wiring are evaluated for safety and capacity, since student and professional tenants run more electronics than these houses were built for. Every house includes working smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, GFCI protection where code requires it and good locks. Consistent materials shorten turns and simplify maintenance.

sections.h2: Student rentals near the University of Arkansas
sections.body:
Houses leased to students near campus need a different level of durability. Roommate households put more wear on kitchens, baths, flooring and doors than a typical family does, and turnover tends to bunch up around the end of the academic year and late summer. Renovations here should favor commercial-grade hardware, solid-core doors, scratch-resistant flooring, durable counters and bathroom fans and fixtures that hold up to heavy use.

Layout matters too. Students value bedrooms of similar size, enough bathrooms and shared space for cooking and studying. Before adding bedrooms or reconfiguring a house, confirm what the city's zoning and occupancy rules allow for unrelated tenants, along with the egress, smoke alarm and electrical requirements for any new sleeping room. Parking is another practical issue on narrow streets near campus. We help you plan renovations that fit the rules and the student market so the house can compete with newer purpose-built student housing in the area.

sections.h2: Turns timed to the Fayetteville calendar
sections.body:
Fayetteville's rental calendar is shaped by the university. Many leases end and begin around late summer, which compresses a large share of turns into a short window. Landlords who wait until move-out to plan the work often find trades booked and materials delayed. We plan turns ahead of that peak: inspecting occupied houses in the spring where access allows, ordering materials early and lining up crews before move-out dates.

After a tenant leaves, a field inspection documents condition with photos and produces a scope against your standard, with tenant damage distinguished from normal wear for deposit purposes. Each turn is also a chance to check for water in lower levels, freeze damage from the past winter, roof wear from spring storms and signs of foundation movement. Crews work in a fixed sequence, you approve the scope and follow progress remotely, and payment follows completed work. Genstone Field Services can handle inspections and occupied maintenance during the year so the late-summer turn list stays manageable.

faqs.q: Can you handle a large batch of Fayetteville turns in late summer?
faqs.a: Yes, with planning. We recommend scheduling inspections and ordering materials before tenants move out, so crews are lined up when units become vacant. Units with the most work start first, and lighter turns are scheduled around them. Genstone Field Services can also handle make-ready work, inspections and occupied maintenance during the year, which keeps the late-summer list shorter and more predictable.

faqs.q: What should a Fayetteville rental renovation include?
faqs.a: Most rental renovations here should address drainage and moisture in lower levels, roof condition, HVAC that handles both heat and cold, electrical capacity and safety, plumbing including freeze protection and durable interior finishes. Houses built before 1978 also require lead-safe practices when painted surfaces are disturbed. We price each item separately so you can decide what to do now and what can wait until a later turn.

faqs.q: Do you work on rentals in Springdale, Rogers and Bentonville?
faqs.a: Yes. We coordinate vetted, licensed local contractors across Northwest Arkansas and handle permits in each city. Houses in Springdale and Rogers often date from the 1970s through the 1990s and need systems, roof and finish updates rather than structural work. A consistent rental standard keeps materials and quality uniform across your portfolio, whether a house is near campus or across the county line.

multifamily-renovation.title: Duplex & 2–4 Unit Renovation in Fayetteville | Genstone
multifamily-renovation.metaDescription: Fayetteville, AR duplex, triplex and fourplex renovation near campus: worn student units rebuilt, shared systems replaced and work timed to the lease cycle.
multifamily-renovation.h1: Duplex and Small Multifamily Renovation in Fayetteville, AR
multifamily-renovation.intro: Fayetteville has more small multifamily buildings than most cities its size, largely because of the university. Duplexes, triplexes and fourplexes built from the 1960s through the 1990s fill streets north and west of campus and around Haskell Heights, and older houses near downtown have been divided into apartments over the years. Many of these buildings have been rented to students continuously for decades with quick turns and little reinvestment. Genstone renovates 2–4 unit buildings for investors who want to raise rents, lower maintenance costs and compete with newer student housing. We phase work around the academic lease cycle, coordinate vetted, licensed local trades and handle City of Fayetteville permits and zoning questions. A designated field manager documents each unit and shared system from start to finish.

sections.h2: Bringing tired student buildings back to market
sections.body:
A typical older duplex or fourplex near campus shows its years of student use: damaged doors and trim, worn or mismatched flooring, kitchens and baths patched rather than renovated, HVAC units near the end of their life, and electrical systems strained by modern loads. Exterior siding, decks and stairs may be weathered or unsafe. Newer complexes with amenities compete for the same tenants, so older buildings need a meaningful upgrade to hold or raise rents.

We start with the building as a whole: roof, siding, decks, stairs, drainage, the electrical service, the sewer line and fire safety between units. Then we renovate units to a repeatable standard with durable flooring, washable finishes, solid doors and hardware, updated kitchens and baths and efficient HVAC. Using the same materials and fixtures in every unit simplifies future repairs and turns. Each building-level item and unit scope is priced separately so you can compare the renovation cost with the rent increase it supports and decide on the right level of investment.

sections.h2: Zoning, unit counts and occupancy near campus
sections.body:
Before renovating a small multifamily building in Fayetteville, confirm what the city recognizes. Some buildings near campus have extra units or bedrooms that were added without permits, and zoning rules affect how many units a lot may contain and how many unrelated people may live in each one. Those limits can change your rent projections significantly.

We check permit history where available, look for signs of unpermitted conversions and help you understand what work would be needed to bring the building into compliance. Adding a bedroom or unit may require egress windows, fire separation, smoke and carbon monoxide alarms and electrical upgrades, and in some cases it may not be allowed at all under current zoning. Older houses divided into apartments near downtown or in historic areas may also face restrictions on exterior changes. Our Pre-Offer Rehab Review identifies these issues before you buy, so your offer reflects the building's legal use rather than the way it has been rented in the past.

sections.h2: Working around the academic lease cycle
sections.body:
Most student buildings in Fayetteville turn over around late summer, which leaves a short window to renovate units between tenants. Trying to do full renovations on several units during that window without planning can push work past move-in dates. We spread the work across the year instead.

Exterior projects such as roofing, siding, decks, drainage and paint can be completed while tenants are in place, ideally in spring or early fall when weather is favorable. Shared-system work like sewer line replacement or electrical service upgrades is scheduled with notice and brief shutoffs. Unit interiors are prioritized by condition, with the most extensive work started as soon as tenants move out and materials ordered well in advance. In buildings constructed before 1978, lead-safe practices protect occupants of nearby units. Your field manager coordinates schedules with you or your property manager and documents progress so you can track which units are ready to lease.

faqs.q: Can you renovate a Fayetteville student fourplex without losing a semester of rent?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. We do exterior and shared-system work while tenants are in place, then renovate unit interiors as leases end, starting with the units that need the most work. Ordering materials before move-out and lining up crews in advance helps finish units before the next lease begins. Where a unit needs more time, your field manager tells you early so leasing can adjust.

faqs.q: What should I check before buying a duplex near the University of Arkansas?
faqs.a: Confirm the legal unit count, zoning and occupancy limits, and check for unpermitted bedrooms or conversions. Then evaluate the roof, siding, decks and stairs, the electrical service, HVAC units, the sewer line, drainage and fire separation between units. Our Pre-Offer Rehab Review estimates the cost of these items so you can compare them with realistic rents before making an offer.

faqs.q: Do you renovate older houses divided into apartments near downtown Fayetteville?
faqs.a: Yes. Older conversions often need structural and drainage work, electrical upgrades, separated utilities and better fire separation between units, and some sit on sloped lots with wet lower levels. We evaluate those items before planning finishes and list each one separately, so you can decide whether to keep the building as apartments or restore it to fewer units. Location near Dickson Street often favors keeping the units.

fha-203k.title: FHA 203(k) Contractor in Fayetteville, AR | Genstone
fha-203k.metaDescription: FHA 203(k) certified contractor in Fayetteville, AR: bids and draws for buyers, agents and lenders on older homes near downtown, Wilson Park and campus.
fha-203k.h1: FHA 203(k) Renovation Contractor in Fayetteville, AR
fha-203k.intro: For many buyers in Fayetteville, an older house that needs work is the only realistic path into a neighborhood like Wilson Park, Mount Sequoyah or the streets near downtown. Those houses often need roofs, HVAC, electrical and plumbing updates, and drainage or foundation repairs before a lender will finance them. An FHA 203(k) loan lets an owner-occupant buyer finance the purchase and the renovation together. Genstone Construction holds FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor status and works with buyers, agents, loan officers and 203(k) consultants across Northwest Arkansas. We prepare detailed bids that fit the program and the house, including the drainage and site work hillside properties often need. After closing, a designated field manager coordinates vetted, licensed local trades, handles City of Fayetteville permits and documents every draw.

sections.h2: Limited or Standard 203(k) on a Fayetteville house
sections.body:
The Limited 203(k) is reserved for non-structural repairs and has a ceiling of $75,000. It can work for a Wilson Park cottage or a mid-century ranch that needs a new roof, HVAC, electrical and plumbing updates, flooring, a kitchen or bath and similar improvements without structural changes.

The Standard 203(k) is required when the work is structural, such as foundation repair, rebuilding rotted framing, replacing a failing retaining wall that affects the house, additions or significant layout changes. It requires a HUD-approved 203(k) consultant, and repairs must total at least $5,000. Hillside houses in Mount Sequoyah, Mount Nord and Washington-Willow often end up in the Standard program once water damage, foundation work or retaining walls are identified. We help buyers and agents determine which version fits at the first walk-through, ideally before the offer. That early decision prevents the delays that come from discovering structural work after the inspection and having to change loan type, rewrite the bid and move the closing date.

sections.h2: Fayetteville houses that fit the program
sections.body:
Good 203(k) candidates in Fayetteville are often older houses in desirable locations that have been held for a long time without major updates. A Wilson Park cottage with original wiring, an aging furnace and a dated kitchen is a typical Limited 203(k). A mid-century ranch in Haskell Heights or on the east side with a worn roof and old systems can be a good fit for a buyer who wants an established neighborhood near campus. Older homes on Mount Sequoyah or near downtown may require a Standard 203(k) for drainage and structural work but offer location and character that new construction cannot.

More difficult properties include worn-out former student rentals with unpermitted bedrooms, houses with serious water problems on steep lots and properties needing extensive excavation or retaining wall work in rocky ground. These can still work, but they require careful evaluation so the renovation fits within the loan and the after-repair appraisal. Lead-based paint rules apply to houses built before 1978, which covers most of Fayetteville's older in-town neighborhoods.

Our 203(k) bids are written for everyone who has to rely on them: the lender's underwriter, the consultant on Standard loans and the buyer. We break out labor and materials by trade, describe each repair in plain language, include quantities where they matter and attach a draw schedule tied to completed stages. On Standard loans, we coordinate with the consultant so the bid and the work write-up match before the package goes to underwriting.

After closing, work on a Fayetteville house usually starts outside and underneath: drainage, structural repair and any retaining wall work, followed by the roof, HVAC, electrical and plumbing, then finishes. Each draw request comes with photos and a completion summary, and funds are released only after the consultant or lender confirms the work. Winter weather can affect exterior and concrete work, so we plan those items with the season in mind. Your field manager handles permits and inspections, the buyer pays nothing upfront and the final payment follows completion and approval.

faqs.q: Can a 203(k) loan cover drainage and retaining wall work in Fayetteville?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Gutters, grading and drainage improvements can be part of a 203(k) scope, and rebuilding a retaining wall that affects the house or replacing rotted framing is structural work that usually calls for the Standard program with a consultant. On hillside houses, we describe these items clearly in the bid so the lender and consultant understand why they are needed to protect the rest of the renovation.

faqs.q: Is a 203(k) a good option for buying in Wilson Park or near downtown?
faqs.a: It can be. Many buyers use a 203(k) to purchase an older house in a desirable neighborhood that needs updates the buyer could not otherwise pay for. The key is choosing a house where the purchase price plus repairs fits within the loan and the after-repair appraisal. We walk the house with the buyer or agent and prepare a bid so they can make that decision before committing.

faqs.q: When should a Fayetteville agent bring Genstone into a 203(k) deal?
faqs.a: As soon as the buyer has a target house, and before the offer if timing allows. An early walk-through lets us flag structural, drainage or site issues that affect whether the buyer needs the Limited or Standard version. Clear pricing helps the buyer decide whether to proceed and keeps closing on schedule. After closing, our field manager keeps the agent, lender and buyer informed through each draw.

reo-renovation.title: REO & Bank-Owned Renovation in Fayetteville, AR | Genstone
reo-renovation.metaDescription: REO renovation in Fayetteville, AR for servicers, banks and GSEs: freeze, water and wear damage repaired on vacant houses and rentals, with full documentation.
reo-renovation.h1: REO and Bank-Owned Property Renovation in Fayetteville, AR
reo-renovation.intro: Bank-owned inventory in Fayetteville tends to be scattered rather than concentrated, and the properties that do come through often have a specific set of problems: houses that sat through a Northwest Arkansas winter without heat and split their pipes, hillside homes with water in the lower level, and former student rentals worn down by years of hard use. Because the regional market is active, a well-prepared REO can attract strong interest from both owner-occupants and investors. Genstone works with mortgage servicers, banks, REITs, investment funds and Government-Sponsored Enterprises, for which we are a preferred contractor, to secure, stabilize and renovate REO properties across Fayetteville and Northwest Arkansas. Genstone Field Services covers preservation, inspections and code compliance, and our renovation team prices and completes repairs through vetted, licensed local trades, documenting every step for asset managers and investor reporting.

sections.h2: Winter, water and vacancy in Northwest Arkansas
sections.body:
Vacant houses in Fayetteville face risks that differ from those in southern markets. Winters bring hard freezes and ice storms, and a house without heat or proper winterization can lose supply lines, water heaters, fixtures and even ceilings and floors when pipes burst and run unnoticed. Ice and wind can damage roofs and bring down trees onto houses. In spring, heavy rain on sloped lots drives water into basements and crawlspaces, feeding mold and rot.

Our first visit produces a photo-documented condition report that separates urgent hazards from the full repair list. We look for freeze damage, active leaks, standing water, mold, roof and tree damage, foundation and retaining wall movement, theft and signs of unauthorized entry. Stabilization can include winterization, shutting off and draining damaged plumbing, tarping or repairing roofs, drying out lower levels, removing wet materials and securing the property. This documentation supports insurance claims for damage during the holding period and gives asset managers a clear basis for choosing between an as-is sale and repairs.

sections.h2: Preservation and code compliance in Fayetteville
sections.body:
The City of Fayetteville enforces property maintenance standards, and vacant properties with tall grass, debris, open structures or damaged exteriors can draw notices. Neighborhoods near campus and downtown are closely watched by residents, which can bring complaints quickly. Genstone Field Services handles preservation tasks that keep properties compliant: securing, boarding when needed, debris removal, lawn care, gutter cleaning, winterization and regular condition checks.

Once the city issues a notice, we log the deadline, finish the corrective work, photograph it and set up the reinspection. If permitted work is needed, such as roofing, structural repair or electrical work, our field manager pulls permits through the city and schedules inspections. Former student rentals sometimes carry unpermitted bedrooms or units, and we flag those during the initial inspection so asset managers can decide whether to correct them before listing or disclose them to investor buyers. Consistent preservation protects the property's value and reduces the chance of new violations while it is held or marketed.

sections.h2: Repair options for an active market
sections.body:
Because Fayetteville has steady demand, the right repair scope can significantly affect recovery. An older house in Wilson Park or near downtown may justify drainage correction, a roof, updated systems and cosmetic work so it can sell to owner-occupants with FHA or conventional financing. A worn duplex near campus may sell best to investors with safety, code and weatherproofing items handled and the rest left to the buyer. A newer house on the edge of town may need only cleaning, paint, flooring and minor repairs.

We price several options so asset managers can compare them with broker price opinions and expected recovery. Each option includes labor, materials, debris removal and dumpsters and is ordered by priority from safety and code items through weatherproofing and systems to cosmetic work. Completed work is documented with photos, and lien waivers and contractor compliance paperwork accompany each payment. If a buyer's inspection turns up new items, the same field manager can price and complete them, which helps keep Washington County files moving toward closing.

faqs.q: What damage is most common in vacant Fayetteville houses?
faqs.a: Freeze damage to plumbing and fixtures, water in basements and crawlspaces on sloped lots, mold, roof and tree damage from ice and spring storms and heavy wear in former student rentals are the most frequent findings. Our first inspection documents each with photos and separates emergency items, such as active leaks or open entries, so the asset manager can approve that work quickly.

faqs.q: Can Genstone winterize and maintain REO properties in Fayetteville?
faqs.a: Yes. Genstone Field Services handles winterization, securing, lawn care, debris removal, gutter cleaning and regular condition checks on vacant properties across Northwest Arkansas. Winterization is especially important here because hard freezes and ice storms can cause major plumbing damage in unheated houses. Regular checks help catch problems early and provide documentation for asset managers and insurers. We can also shut off and drain systems on short notice when a cold front is forecast.

faqs.q: Do you work with servicers and GSEs on Northwest Arkansas REO files?
faqs.a: Yes. Servicers, banks, REITs, investment funds and other lenders use Genstone for REO work, and the company is a preferred contractor for Government-Sponsored Enterprises. Each Fayetteville file includes condition reports, priced repair options, photos of completed work, lien waivers and contractor compliance records, so reviewers can follow every decision from first inspection to closing. Field Services handles preservation on the same files.
